items.prompt: State the function of the valve tendons attached to the flaps of an atrioventricular valve.
items.canonical_answer: The tendons stop the flaps of the valve being forced back into the atrium when the ventricle contracts.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the function stated, that the tendons hold the flaps so that they are not pushed back (turned inside out) into the atrium as the ventricle contracts and the blood pushes on them.

This is a structure and function point: naming the tendons without their function earns no mark, and saying that the tendons open or close the valve is a confusion, because the pressure of the blood moves the flaps.

items.prompt: Describe how the atrioventricular valve on the left side of the heart is shut when the left ventricle contracts, and how it is kept from turning inside out.
items.canonical_answer: As the ventricle contracts, the pressure of the blood in it rises above the pressure in the left atrium, which pushes the flaps of the valve together and shuts it. The valve tendons, fixed to the papillary muscles, hold the edges of the flaps so that they are not forced back into the atrium.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: (1) how it shuts: ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure and the blood pushes the flaps together; (2) how it is held: the tendons attached to the flaps stop them being forced back into the atrium.
The reason must be pressure of blood, because the valve has no muscle of its own that closes it; a statement that the valve contracts earns no mark for the first point.

items.prompt: A learner says that the coronary arteries are the aorta and the pulmonary artery, because they are the arteries that leave the heart. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is a confusion of two sets of vessels. The aorta and the pulmonary artery are the major vessels that carry blood out of the ventricles, to the body and to the lungs. The coronary arteries are different: narrow vessels that branch from the aorta near its base and run over the surface of the heart, supplying the cardiac muscle of the heart wall with oxygenated blood. The test is to ask which vessels feed the heart's own muscle; those are the coronary arteries.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that the major vessels leaving the heart are wrongly called the coronary arteries (1); the correct idea, that the coronary arteries branch from the aorta and supply the heart muscle itself, or the test question that tells them apart (1).
The card is a discrimination between the two, not a repeat of the definition of the aorta. The key words for the second mark are heart muscle and branch from the aorta.

items.prompt: A learner is making a plan diagram of a heart cut lengthwise. State one feature that the diagram should show about the walls of the left ventricle and the right ventricle.
items.canonical_answer: The wall of the left ventricle should be drawn clearly thicker than the wall of the right ventricle, in proportion to the specimen.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one feature, that the left ventricle wall is drawn thicker than the right ventricle wall in proportion to the specimen (a typical ratio of about three to one is also credited).

Credit also that both ventricle walls are drawn thicker than the atrial walls. A statement about shading, colour or drawing single muscle cells earns no mark, because a plan diagram has none of these.

items.prompt: A learner makes a plan diagram of a heart cut lengthwise. In the diagram the wall of the left ventricle and the wall of the right ventricle are drawn the same thickness, and a few single muscle cells are drawn in the wall of the left atrium. Explain why each of these two features is a fault in a plan diagram.
items.canonical_answer: The equal wall thickness is a fault because a plan diagram records the proportions of the specimen, and in the specimen the left ventricle wall is clearly thicker than the right. The single cells are a fault because a plan diagram is a low-power outline of tissues and cavities, so it contains no individual cells.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: (1) equal thickness is a fault because the diagram must record the proportions and the left ventricle wall is thicker than the right; (2) single cells are a fault because a plan diagram outlines tissues and does not show cells.
Each fault must be linked to the given diagram with a reason, because naming the fault alone earns no mark; this case needs both the feature and the reason.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the term myocardium.
items.canonical_answer: The myocardium is the cardiac muscle that forms the walls of the heart chambers.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the term means the cardiac muscle of the heart wall. The key words are cardiac muscle and wall.
A definition that says only 'the heart' or 'the heart tissue' is too vague; coronary arteries and valves are not the myocardium.

items.prompt: Explain why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than the wall of the right ventricle.
items.canonical_answer: The left ventricle sends blood around the whole body at a high pressure, so it needs a thick wall of cardiac muscle to contract forcefully. The right ventricle sends the same volume of blood only to the nearby lungs at a much lower pressure, so a thinner wall is enough, and a higher pressure would risk damaging the thin lung capillaries.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: (1) the left ventricle pumps to the whole body, so it must produce a higher pressure; (2) a thicker wall means more cardiac muscle and a more forceful contraction, whereas the right ventricle pumps to the nearby lungs at a lower pressure, which protects the lung capillaries.
The difference is about pressure and distance: a statement that the left ventricle pumps more blood than the right is wrong, because both pump about the same volume per beat.

items.prompt: Describe the order of the three stages of the cardiac cycle, starting from the stage when the whole heart is relaxed, and say what happens to the blood in each stage.
items.canonical_answer: First, in diastole, the heart is relaxed and blood flows from the veins into the atria and on through the open atrioventricular valves into the ventricles. Then, in atrial systole, the atria contract and push the last of the blood into the ventricles. Finally, in ventricular systole, the ventricles contract and force blood out into the aorta and the pulmonary artery. The result is that blood moves one way, from the veins to the arteries.
marking_guidance: 3 marks, one for each stage in the correct order: diastole (relaxed, atria and ventricles fill), atrial systole (atria contract, blood pushed into ventricles), ventricular systole (ventricles contract, blood forced into the arteries).

The sequence is the point: a stage out of order, or the stages named without what happens to the blood, earns no mark for that stage. The end result of one-way flow is a creditworthy point but the tariff is 3.

items.prompt: Describe how the pressure in the left ventricle causes the semilunar valve at the base of the aorta to open and then to close during one cardiac cycle.
items.canonical_answer: As the left ventricle contracts, its pressure rises above the pressure in the aorta, which forces the semilunar valve open and blood leaves. As the ventricle then relaxes, its pressure falls below the aortic pressure, so blood begins to move back, fills the pockets of the cups and closes the valve.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: (1) opening: ventricular pressure rises above aortic pressure, which forces the valve open; (2) closing: ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure, so blood moves back and fills the pockets, which shuts the valve.
Both marks need the pressure comparison, because the valve is moved by the pressure difference and not by muscle.

items.prompt:
These are our own values for the left side of the heart in one cardiac cycle.

| Time (s) | Left ventricle (kPa) | Aorta (kPa) |
|---|---|---|
| 0.15 | 6.0 | 10.7 |
| 0.20 | 13.0 | 12.0 |
| 0.25 | 16.0 | 15.5 |
| 0.30 | 15.0 | 15.0 |
| 0.35 | 9.0 | 13.0 |

Describe what the table shows about the pressure in the left ventricle compared with the pressure in the aorta between 0.15 s and 0.35 s, and say what this means for the semilunar valve.
items.canonical_answer: At 0.15 s the ventricular pressure, 6.0 kPa, is below the aortic pressure, 10.7 kPa, so the valve is shut. By 0.20 s the ventricular pressure, 13.0 kPa, is above the aortic pressure, 12.0 kPa, which means the valve has opened and blood is leaving the ventricle. By 0.35 s the ventricular pressure, 9.0 kPa, has fallen below the aortic pressure, 13.0 kPa, so the valve has shut again.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: (1) readings from the table that the ventricular pressure is below the aortic pressure at 0.15 s, above it at 0.20 s and below it again at 0.35 s, with values; (2) what it means: the valve is shut, opens when ventricular pressure passes aortic pressure and shuts again when it falls below. The table shows values, and the meaning links them to the valve.
Each reading is quoted with its unit, kPa. A comparison without values, or values without the meaning for the valve, earns one mark at most.

items.prompt: A graph for one person at rest has time in seconds on the horizontal axis and pressure in kPa on the vertical axis. At 0.05 s the line for the left atrium is at 0.5 kPa and the line for the left ventricle is at 0.4 kPa. At 0.20 s the line for the left atrium is at 0.8 kPa and the line for the left ventricle is at 17 kPa. Describe what the graph shows about the pressures in the left atrium and left ventricle at these two times, and say what this means for the atrioventricular valve.
items.canonical_answer: At 0.05 s the atrial pressure, 0.5 kPa, is slightly above the ventricular pressure, 0.4 kPa, so the atrioventricular valve is open and blood flows into the ventricle. At 0.20 s the ventricular pressure, 17 kPa, is far above the atrial pressure, 0.8 kPa, which means the valve is shut, so blood cannot flow back into the atrium.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: (1) the reading at 0.05 s, atrial above ventricular, meaning the valve is open; (2) the reading at 0.20 s, ventricular far above atrial, meaning the valve is shut.
Each reading must come from the graph values with its unit and be linked to the valve state; the values on their own gives one mark at most.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the term pacemaker in the heart.
items.canonical_answer: The pacemaker is the sinoatrial node, a patch of specialised cardiac muscle in the wall of the right atrium that generates the wave of excitation which starts each heartbeat.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the term means the sinoatrial node (SAN) in the wall of the right atrium that starts each beat. The key words are sinoatrial node and starts or initiates the wave of excitation.
The atrioventricular node is not the pacemaker; it passes the wave on after a delay.

items.prompt: Explain how the atrioventricular node makes sure that the atria have finished contracting before the ventricles begin to contract.
items.canonical_answer: The wave of excitation from the sinoatrial node cannot cross the layer of fibrous tissue between the atria and the ventricles, so it reaches the ventricles through the atrioventricular node, the one route across. The node delays the wave by about 0.1 s before passing it on, which gives the atria time to empty into the ventricles before the ventricles contract.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: (1) the fibrous tissue does not conduct, so the wave must pass through the atrioventricular node; (2) the node delays the wave (about 0.1 s) which allows the atria to finish emptying into the ventricles first.
The delay is the cause of the timing, so a statement that the node starts the heartbeat earns no mark; that is the role of the sinoatrial node.

items.prompt: A patient has damage to the Purkyne tissue in the walls of the ventricles, so the wave of excitation cannot travel quickly through it. The sinoatrial node and the atrioventricular node work normally. Explain why the ventricles are likely to pump blood less effectively in this case.
items.canonical_answer: Normally the Purkyne tissue conducts the wave quickly down the septum to the apex and up the ventricle walls, so the ventricles contract together from the apex upwards and squeeze blood towards the arteries. With this damage the wave would spread slowly from cell to cell, so the contraction would be slower and less well coordinated, and less blood would be forced out of the arteries' openings in each beat.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: (1) the normal role, that the Purkyne tissue conducts the wave quickly so that the ventricles contract together from the apex upwards; (2) the effect, that without it the wave spreads slowly, so the contraction is slower and less coordinated and pushes less blood out.

The answer must be applied to the case given, because the sinoatrial node and the atrioventricular node are stated to work normally; credit the likely effect, since the exact outcome in a patient varies.

items.prompt:
Twelve questions. Choose one option for each.

1. Which vessel carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body?
A  vena cava
B  pulmonary artery
C  aorta
D  pulmonary vein

2. Which vessels supply the muscle of the heart wall with blood?
A  the aorta and the pulmonary artery
B  the pulmonary veins
C  the coronary arteries
D  the vena cava

3. What is the function of the valve tendons?
A  to pump blood into the ventricle
B  to stop the flaps of an atrioventricular valve being forced back into the atrium
C  to open the semilunar valves
D  to carry the wave of excitation to the ventricles

4. Which statement about the walls of the ventricles is correct?
A  The right ventricle wall is thicker than the left because the lungs are far away.
B  The atrial walls are thicker than the ventricle walls because atria pump blood further.
C  The left ventricle wall is thicker than the right because it pumps blood at a higher pressure around the body.
D  The two ventricle walls are the same thickness because they pump the same volume of blood.

5. Why are the walls of the atria thin?
A  An atrium pushes blood only a short distance into a ventricle at low pressure.
B  An atrium pumps blood to the lungs at a high pressure.
C  An atrium has no cardiac muscle.
D  An atrium needs to expand to fill with oxygen.

6. Which feature belongs in a plan diagram of a heart cut lengthwise?
A  individual muscle cells drawn in the wall
B  the outlines of the chambers and walls in proportion, with no individual cells
C  shading to show the thickness of the walls
D  a high-power view of a single valve flap

7. Which row is correct while blood is being forced out of the ventricles into the arteries?
A  atrioventricular valves open and semilunar valves closed
B  atrioventricular valves closed and semilunar valves open
C  both sets of valves open
D  both sets of valves closed

8. What causes an atrioventricular valve to close?
A  contraction of the valve flaps themselves
B  ventricular pressure rising above atrial pressure
C  aortic pressure rising above atrial pressure
D  the tendons pulling the flaps open

9. These are our own values. At 0.15 s the left ventricle pressure is 6.0 kPa and the aortic pressure is 10.7 kPa. What is the state of the semilunar valve and why?
A  open because the ventricle pressure is below the aortic pressure
B  closed because the ventricle pressure is below the aortic pressure
C  open because the ventricle pressure is above the aortic pressure
D  closed because the ventricle pressure is above the atrial pressure

10. A graph of left ventricle pressure against time shows a steep rise starting at 0.10 s and a steep fall to near 1.5 kPa at 0.40 s. How long does ventricular systole last on this graph?
A  0.10 s
B  0.30 s
C  0.40 s
D  0.80 s

11. In which order does the wave of excitation pass through the heart?
A  sinoatrial node, atrioventricular node, Purkyne tissue
B  atrioventricular node, sinoatrial node, Purkyne tissue
C  sinoatrial node, Purkyne tissue, atrioventricular node
D  Purkyne tissue, sinoatrial node, atrioventricular node

12. What is the effect of the delay at the atrioventricular node?
A  The atria finish emptying into the ventricles before the ventricles contract.
B  The ventricles contract before the atria.
C  The blood in the ventricles receives more oxygen.
D  The wave of excitation stops.
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 C, 2 C, 3 B, 4 C, 5 A, 6 B, 7 B, 8 B, 9 B, 10 B, 11 A, 12 A.
1. The aorta leaves the left ventricle (C). A is the vessel that brings blood into the right atrium; B leaves the right ventricle and carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs; D brings blood into the left atrium.
2. The coronary arteries branch from the aorta and supply the heart muscle (C). A is the register error of calling the vessels that leave the heart the coronary arteries; B and D bring blood into the chambers and do not feed the muscle.
3. The tendons hold the flaps (B). A gives them the role of the muscle; C confuses the two valves; D confuses the tendons with the Purkyne tissue.
4. The left ventricle produces the higher pressure (C). A reverses the comparison and misjudges the distance; B reverses atria and ventricles; D takes the true statement about equal volume and wrongly concludes equal thickness.
5. A short distance and a low pressure need little muscle (A). B gives the atrium the job of the ventricle; C is wrong because atrial walls contain cardiac muscle; D confuses the heart with the lungs.
6. A plan diagram outlines tissues and cavities in proportion (B). A is a feature of a high-power drawing; C is shading, which a plan diagram does not use; D is high power, whereas a plan diagram is low power.
7. During ventricular systole the high ventricular pressure shuts the atrioventricular valves and opens the semilunar valves (B). A is the arrangement during diastole; C would allow blood to flow backwards into the atria; D would leave the blood no way out.
8. The pressure of blood in the ventricle pushes the flaps shut (B). A gives the valve muscle it does not have; C compares the wrong vessel, since the aorta is not connected to the atrioventricular valve; D reverses what the tendons do.
9. The ventricle pressure is below the aortic pressure, so the valve is shut (B). A has the right comparison with the wrong state; C describes a comparison that is not true at this time; D mixes up the two valves.
10. The rise starts at 0.10 s and the fall finishes at 0.40 s, a duration of 0.30 s (B). A is the time of the start, C is the time of the end, and D is the whole cycle.
11. The wave starts at the sinoatrial node, is delayed at the atrioventricular node and then spreads along the Purkyne tissue (A). B, C and D put the structures in orders that would start the beat in the wrong place or send the wave to the ventricles before the atria.
12. The delay gives the atria time to empty (A). B reverses the sequence; C confuses the heart with the lungs; D is wrong because the wave passes on after about 0.1 s.
marking_guidance: The key: one mark per correct option, twelve marks in all; about half the questions test recall and half test application to a described graph, table, sequence or structure.

Each distractor is a named error: the major vessels called the coronary arteries (the misconception register first), the roles of the two valves swapped, valves said to have their own muscle, the thicker wall put on the wrong ventricle, and the nodes put in the wrong order.

items.prompt:
A class in Windhoek studied the left side of a heart. These are our own values for one cardiac cycle.

| Time (s) | Left atrium (kPa) | Left ventricle (kPa) | Aorta (kPa) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.10 | 1.0 | 0.9 | 10.7 |
| 0.15 | 0.5 | 6.0 | 10.7 |
| 0.25 | 1.0 | 16.0 | 15.5 |
| 0.35 | 1.5 | 9.0 | 13.0 |
| 0.50 | 1.0 | 0.8 | 11.5 |

(a) State the highest pressure in the left ventricle shown in the table. [1]
(b) Describe how the table shows that the atrioventricular valve is shut at 0.15 s. [2]
(c) Explain why the aortic pressure at 0.50 s is much higher than the ventricular pressure, although blood does not flow from the aorta into the ventricle. [2]
(d) Suggest, using values from the table, why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than the wall of the left atrium. [2]
(e) Name the tissue that carries the wave of excitation quickly through the walls of the ventricles. [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) 16.0 kPa.
(b) At 0.15 s the ventricular pressure, 6.0 kPa, is above the atrial pressure, 0.5 kPa, so the blood in the ventricle pushes the flaps of the valve together and shuts it.
(c) The semilunar valve is shut at 0.50 s, because the ventricular pressure is below the aortic pressure, so blood cannot flow back; the blood held in the aorta keeps the aortic pressure high, and it falls only slowly.
(d) The ventricle reaches 16.0 kPa whereas the atrium reaches only 1.5 kPa, so the ventricle must contract far more forcefully, which needs a thicker wall of cardiac muscle.
(e) Purkyne tissue.
marking_guidance: Marks and points: (a) 1 mark for 16.0 kPa; (b) 2 marks from three points: ventricular pressure 6.0 kPa above atrial pressure 0.5 kPa, so the flaps are pushed together, so the valve is shut; (c) 2 marks from three points: the semilunar valve is shut, because ventricular pressure is lower, so no backflow, and the aortic pressure falls slowly; (d) 2 marks from three points: 16.0 kPa against 1.5 kPa, more forceful contraction is needed, so a thicker wall holds more muscle; (e) 1 mark for Purkyne tissue.

Parts (a) and (e) credit AO A (2 marks); parts (b), (c) and (d) credit AO B (6 marks). Each reason must be written with the given term or value, because a reason without the figures from the table earns no mark in (d).
